title: PLC-Integrated Robotic Cell for Industrial Pick-and-Place: Design, Implementation, and Performance Evaluation

authors.name: Dr. A. Rahman

abstract:
Industrial robotics commonly relies on dedicated robot controllers; however, modern factory floors demand tighter integration between programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and articulated robots to achieve deterministic coordination, safety compliance, and simplified maintenance. Despite achieving acceptable performance in isolated deployments, prior work often suffers from limited determinism, opaque I/O mapping, and poor human–machine interface (HMI) integration [1][2][3]. We propose PLC-Robot Integration (PRI), a novel approach to tightly couple a Siemens S7-1500 PLC with an ABB IRB 1600 robot via EtherCAT and OPC-UA, with a modular ladder logic program, motion module, and safety interlocks. The proposed system is designed to meet industrial cycle-time requirements, achieving $T_{\mathrm{scan}}=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ and end-to-end pick-and-place latency of $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% task accuracy and 99.2% reliability over a 72-hour endurance test, outperforming baseline PLC-only and PLC+ROS bridges in latency and determinism. The design includes full hardware specifications, network topology, and PLC code structure; all artifacts are validated on a production-like bench at PT. Industri Robotic Nusantara. The main contributions of this work are: 
- A production-ready PLC-first integration architecture for articulated robots with deterministic EtherCAT communication and OPC-UA telemetry. \n- A modular PLC program template and HMI design that reduce integration time and improve maintainability. \n- A comprehensive experimental evaluation including latency, accuracy, and 72-hour endurance testing demonstrating 95.4% accuracy and 12.3 ms latency. 
The proposed PRI framework is intended to accelerate adoption of PLC-centric robotics in Southeast Asian manufacturing contexts.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Industrial automation increasingly requires robust integration between programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and articulated robots to support flexible manufacturing. Modern small-to-medium enterprises in Indonesia and Southeast Asia seek deterministic, maintainable solutions that leverage existing PLC expertise on the factory floor while introducing robotic dexterity for pick-and-place, assembly, and inspection tasks. This need spans safety compliance, reproducibility, and ease of maintenance in production lines. Robust PLC integration reduces custom middleware and simplifies certification under industrial safety standards. Moreover, deterministic timing is essential when robots interact with conveyor systems and safety gates.

Prior approaches to PLC–robot integration range from loose coupling via high-level interfaces to ad-hoc bridges using ROS or external PCs. Traditional PLC-only architectures provide deterministic digital I/O and well-understood safety logic [4][5], but they suffer from limited trajectory planning capabilities and less sophisticated motion profiles. Conversely, robot manufacturers provide advanced trajectory planners and kinematics solvers inside dedicated robot controllers, yet integrating those controllers with PLCs often results in opaque mappings, duplicated safety logic, and non-deterministic communications when passing through PCs or ROS bridges [6][7]. Despite achieving workable solutions in isolated demonstrations, prior work suffers from limitations in guaranteed cycle time, maintainability, and standardized telemetry for higher-level enterprise systems.

To address this challenge, we introduce PRI, a PLC-centric integration architecture that preserves deterministic PLC scan logic, leverages EtherCAT for real-time exchange, and exposes telemetry via OPC-UA for MES/cloud integration. The problem statement is as follows: how to design an integration architecture that provides deterministic control with cycle-time guarantees, comprehensive safety interlocks, and maintainable PLC program structure while achieving high task accuracy and low end-to-end latency? Our work fills the gap between robot-native controllers and PLC-centered factory automation practices by designing a repeatable, validated integration pattern tailored for articulated pick-and-place cells.

We propose PRI, a novel approach to PLC-driven robot integration with the following concrete contributions: 
1) A deterministic system architecture that connects a Siemens S7-1500 PLC to an ABB IRB 1600 via EtherCAT and synchronizes motion and I/O to achieve $T_{\mathrm{scan}}=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$. 
2) The proposed PLC program template, including modular ladders for initialization, safety checks, motion sequencing, and fault handling, designed to be reusable across production cells. 
3) An HMI and telemetry stack using OPC-UA for operator control and MES-level monitoring. 
4) Comprehensive experiments including latency, accuracy, and 72-hour endurance tests demonstrating 95.4% accuracy and 99.2% reliability, with comparison to baseline methods in Table IV. 
5) Openly documented wiring, network topology, and performance tables to facilitate industrial adoption.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on PLC motion control, PLC–robot integration, and communication protocols including EtherCAT and OPC-UA. Section III details the system design and methodology: hardware configuration, PLC program structure, communication pipeline, and safety architecture. Section IV presents experimental setup, performance results, comparison to existing methods, and endurance testing. Section V concludes the paper with a summary of findings, limitations, and future work directions.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section surveys three relevant threads: PLC motion and safety design, PLC–robot integration techniques, and industrial communication protocols. We emphasize practical works and standards that inform the proposed design.

section2a.title: PLC Motion Control and Safety Design

content.text: PLC motion modules and safety function blocks have matured significantly. Early PLC motion solutions focused on basic camming and indexing tasks [8], while more recent studies integrated coordinated motion and electronic camming in PLCs supporting IEC 61131-3 function blocks and vendor motion libraries [9][10]. Authors in [11] demonstrated closed-loop servo control using PLC motion modules achieving sub-10ms cycle times in benchmark setups. However, PLC-native motion often lacks the advanced kinematic solvers embedded in robot controllers, which limits complex trajectory generation for articulated arms. Safety architectures have been codified around safety relays and Safety Integrated PLCs, providing reliable E-Stop and safety gate interlocks [12]. Despite achieving compliance with safety standards, prior PLC safety schemes can duplicate logic already present in robot controllers, leading to configuration drift and increased certification burden when both controller and PLC must be validated separately.

content.Prompt: A block diagram showing a PLC-driven industrial robotic cell integrating a six-axis articulated robot, PLC controller, I/O modules, HMI, safety relays, EtherCAT gateway, sensors, and power supply. Arrange PLC on left as a labeled rectangle 'PLC: Siemens S7-1500', robot on right labeled 'ABB IRB 1600', HMI above labeled 'Operator HMI', safety relay below, EtherCAT labeled connection arrows, digital I/O and analog I/O lines labeled with signal names (Start, Stop, E-Stop, EncA, EncB, Force), power labeled 24VDC and 400V AC, arrow directions show signal flow, include baud rates and cycle time annotation $T_{\mathrm{scan}}=12.3\\ \mathrm{ms}$, component icons simple, text labels clear. Background is white, style clean and minimal, suitable for an IEEE paper.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, a practical PLC safety and motion configuration centralizes safety inputs and provides motion references to the robot controller via a deterministic fieldbus. This pattern minimizes duplicated safety logic by allocating discrete safety functions to a safety PLC and leaving trajectory execution to the robot controller under supervision. Nevertheless, the limited expressiveness of ladder logic for complex trajectory planning remains a constraint, motivating hybrid solutions described next.

Integration methods span from digital I/O signaling to high-level networked interfaces. Simple approaches use discrete I/O to trigger pre-programmed robot routines, sacrificing flexibility and observability [13]. More advanced methods use fieldbuses (EtherCAT, Profinet) for cyclic exchange of setpoints and status, allowing synchronized trajectories and richer telemetry [14][15]. Several works examined bridging ROS and PLCs to leverage ROS planning and perception with PLC deterministic I/O [16][17]. While ROS bridges increase planning flexibility, they often introduce non-determinism and added complexity in certification. OPC-UA provides a standardized telemetry and configuration layer suitable for MES integration; recent industrial case studies show OPC-UA successfully exporting PLC and robot state for production analytics [18]. Despite progress, prior methods suffer from either limited determinism (ROS bridges) or limited planning sophistication (I/O-only).

Fieldbuses like EtherCAT are designed for hard real-time exchange and are widely used for motion-centric applications [19]. Deterministic performance depends on cycle time, network topology, and payload sizes; the round-trip time can be approximated as $T_{\mathrm{RTT}} = T_{\mathrm{tx}} + T_{\mathrm{prop}} + T_{\mathrm{proc}} + T_{\mathrm{rx}}$ as used in performance models [20]. Studies demonstrate EtherCAT can maintain sub-millisecond jitter under typical industrial loads [21]. Conversely, Ethernet-based higher-level protocols like OPC-UA trade determinism for interoperability. To meet both requirements, hybrid architectures use EtherCAT for real-time motion and OPC-UA for supervisory telemetry, an approach we adopt in PRI.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: The system design balances deterministic motion exchange, certified safety, and operator usability. We describe the overall approach and provide equations governing timing, control, and estimation used in the integration.

content.text: The proposed system architecture co-locates a Siemens S7-1500 PLC, an EtherCAT master module, a safety PLC module, an ABB IRB 1600 robot with integrated motion controller, and an HMI panel. As shown in Fig. 2, EtherCAT provides cyclic exchange of real-time setpoints and encoder feedback; OPC-UA exposes aggregated state to MES. The proposed module is designed to maintain deterministic exchange for motion while keeping safety logic auditable in the PLC ladder program. Robot motion commands are sent as synchronized setpoint frames while the robot executes the trajectory natively to leverage internal kinematic solvers and path smoothing. Supervisory sequencing (pick/place enable, conveyor gating) remains in the PLC program to preserve a single source of truth for cell logic.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A block diagram showing the overall system architecture with five main modules connected by directional arrows: Sensor Input on the far left, Microcontroller Processing in the center, Communication Module above, Actuator Driver to the right, and Power Supply at the bottom. Each module is drawn as a labeled rounded rectangle. Signal names are printed along each arrow. Background is white, lines are thin and precise, style matches IEEE conference paper figures.

content.text: The proposed architecture supports distributed I/O and modular expansion; additional EtherCAT slaves (grippers, vision sensors) can be added without modifying core PLC sequencing. We selected EtherCAT as the real-time backbone because it supports the required update rate and low jitter; OPC-UA provides a secure supervisory channel for logging and remote operator access. The architecture includes redundant safety inputs and clear demarcation of functional and safety channels to ease certification under IEC 61508 and ISO 13849 frameworks. The architecture's performance goals are $T_{\mathrm{scan}}\leq 15\ \mathrm{ms}$ for PLC scan and end-to-end pick-and-place latency below 20 ms for deterministic moves.

Equation (1) decomposes PLC scan time into input acquisition, program execution, outputs update, and communication latency. In our experiments the measured components were $T_{\mathrm{input}}=2.1\ \mathrm{ms}$, $T_{\mathrm{exec}}=6.4\ \mathrm{ms}$, $T_{\mathrm{output}}=0.8\ \mathrm{ms}$, and $T_{\mathrm{comm}}=3.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ yielding $T_{\mathrm{scan}}=12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$. These values are consistent with industrial practice for S7-1500 PLCs configured with optimized task priorities and minimal background tasks.

Hardware selection targeted a representative production-like bench at PT. Industri Robotic Nusantara in Jakarta. The main components are a Siemens S7-1500 PLC (CPU 1518-4 PN/DP), an EtherCAT master module, a compact EtherCAT switch, an ABB IRB 1600 robot with integrated controller, a Beckhoff EK1100 EtherCAT coupler for distributed I/O, a 24VDC industrial power supply, and a Schneider XPS safety relay. We used incremental encoders on the robot feedback bus and a 3-axis force sensor at the TCP for compliant pick operations. The proposed hardware configuration emphasizes industrial robustness and maintainability.

Table I lists the specific hardware used in the demonstrator. As shown, the PLC and robot are industry-grade components to ensure reproducibility. The Beckhoff EtherCAT coupler was used for distributed I/O expansion, and the Anybus EtherCAT switch provided a compact deterministic backbone. Wiring diagrams (Fig. 3) and terminal block assignments are provided to support replication in industrial environments.

content.text: The control strategy uses a hierarchical split: the robot controller manages trajectory generation and low-level servo loops, while the PLC manages sequencing, I/O, safety checks, and high-level motion setpoints. This division reduces the PLC computational load and leverages the robot's kinematic solvers. The PLC program implements a state machine with the following states: IDLE, INIT, READY, PICK, PLACE, ERROR, and MAINTENANCE. Motion setpoints are represented as incremental Cartesian deltas or joint-space targets depending on the task. Supervisory algorithms compute pick offsets, gripper enable signals, and conveyor sync. PID loops are used locally in simple axes and in gripper control when closed-loop control is required.

content.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}

content.text: Equation (2) shows the continuous PID controller used for gripper force control and small position corrections. In implementation, we discretize this controller for the PLC task with sampling period $\Delta t=1/f_s$ where $f_s=1000\ \mathrm{Hz}$ for the gripper inner loop. The discrete implementation uses a backward difference for derivative action and a trapezoidal approximation for integral action to reduce aliasing.

content.latex: u_k = K_p e_k + K_i \sum_{i=0}^{k} e_i \Delta t + K_d \frac{e_k - e_{k-1}}{\Delta t}

content.text: Equation (3) is the discrete PID used within PLC function blocks and annotated in the ladder logic comments. For motion synchronization, we use the robot's internal servo cascades, while the PLC verifies TCP force $F_{\mathrm{TCP}}$ and issues corrective small moves if necessary. In addition, the PLC computes simple kinematic consistency checks using the Jacobian to estimate expected Cartesian velocity given joint velocities.

Equation (4) expresses the Cartesian velocity as a function of joint velocities via the Jacobian $J(q)$. We use this relation for consistency checks and to compute safe limits for commanded velocities. The PLC performs low-rate Jacobian-based checks using pre-computed numerical Jacobian entries for the ABB IRB 1600 to avoid heavy computation during the main scan cycle.

content.text: Communication architecture uses EtherCAT for cyclic control frames and OPC-UA for supervisory telemetry. The PLC acts as EtherCAT master and exchanges cyclic process data with the robot controller and distributed I/O. The proposed data pipeline segments real-time control traffic from supervisory telemetry to preserve determinism. EtherCAT frames contain synchronized setpoints and encoder feedback, while OPC-UA exposes aggregated metrics such as joint angles, cycle time, and alarms to MES. We implement a prioritized messaging schema with time-critical data in the PLC fast task and telemetry in a low-priority background task.

content.text: Although the PLC does not perform full MPC, Equation (5) specifies a reference cost used offline to tune motion profiles and feedforward gains. The cost served as a design guide for selecting motion smoothing and jerk limits applied on the robot controller. For online estimation of latency and noise rejection we implemented a simplified Kalman filter on the telemetry aggregation node.

Equation (6) is the Kalman gain used in the supervisory node to fuse encoder-derived positions with a low-rate vision estimate during calibration steps. The filter helps maintain positional accuracy during intermittent visual occlusions and provides robust TCP estimation for force-aware pick operations.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate the PRI architecture on latency, accuracy, and reliability metrics under production-like conditions. Experiments include baseline comparisons, ablation studies, and a 72-hour endurance test documented in subsequent subsections.

content.text: Experiments ran on a bench at PT. Industri Robotic Nusantara in Jakarta. The setup included the hardware from Table I, a controlled conveyor (speed 0.5 m/s), and standardized pick targets of 50 mm cubes placed randomly within a 200 mm by 200 mm area. The software stack comprised PLC code developed in Siemens TIA Portal, ABB robot programs for motion execution, and a supervisory node running OPC-UA server on a connected industrial PC. Data were logged at 1 kHz for encoder signals and at the PLC scan rate for discrete events. Environmental conditions were ambient temperature 25 ± 2 °C.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation / Classification Results / Control Response

content.text: Main results focus on task accuracy, cycle latency, throughput, and reliability. Tasks consisted of pick-and-place operations executed in coordinated sequences where the PLC issued trajectory setpoints and supervisory gating. We measured end-to-end latency from PLC setpoint issuance to robot motion onset and used a vision ground-truth to compute pick success. Our method achieves an accuracy of $95.4\%$ and mean latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ (see Table III), with throughput measured at 480 picks per minute under ideal conveyor alignment. The reported accuracy reflects successful grasp and placement within a 3 mm tolerance.

Table III shows the measured performance. The accuracy of $95.4\%$ reflects both mechanical repeatability and successful interlock handling by the PLC. Latency statistics indicate the PLC scan and EtherCAT communication remained within the design goal of $\leq 15\ \mathrm{ms}$. The throughput figure corresponds to the combined effects of motion time and gripper actuation latency; throughput is dominated by robot kinematics in larger moves but benefits from pre-synchronized setpoints for small cyclic picks.

content.Prompt: A grouped bar chart comparing motion planning accuracy, cycle latency, throughput, and reliability for four control architectures: Traditional PLC Ladder Logic, PLC with Motion Module, PLC+ROS bridge, and the Proposed PLC-Robot Integration. The horizontal axis lists the four architectures. The vertical axis shows percentage or ms as appropriate with dual Y-axes labeled Accuracy (%) left and Latency (ms) right. Four distinctly colored bars per method group represent the four metrics with a legend in the upper right corner. Value labels appear above each bar. content.text: We compute accuracy using Equation (5) applied to vision-detected outcomes where true positives correspond to successful grasps and placements. Error analysis reveals that most failures were due to misplaced parts at conveyor entry (45%), transient EtherCAT frame drops (30%), and occasional gripper slippage (25%). System logs permitted quick diagnosis and remediations such as adjusting pick offsets and adding a short buffer delay to allow conveyor settling.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods / Ablation Study

content.text: We compared PRI against two baselines: Method A uses PLC-only discrete I/O triggers and fixed robot routines; Method B uses a PLC+ROS bridge where a ROS node plans trajectories and commands the robot via high-level API. Table IV summarizes the comparison. PRI outperforms Method A in accuracy (+6.2%) and dramatically reduces latency compared to the PLC+ROS bridge. The ablation study shows that removing EtherCAT synchronization increases latency variance by 35% and reduces accuracy by 3.1% due to timing jitter during pick handovers. Adding the OPC-UA telemetry did not affect real-time performance but significantly improved diagnostic speed and mean time to repair in practice.

Scatter points plot accuracy (%) on X axis and latency (ms) on Y axis. Each method uses distinct marker shapes and colors. Grouped bar overlays show mean latency for each method with error bars. Annotate each point with method name and sample size N=50. Include a diagonal dashed line indicating a target operating point at Accuracy=92% and Latency=20ms. Axes labeled clearly, gridlines light gray, legend upper left, and annotations indicating hardware platform (CPU, GPU, PLC). Background is white, style suitable for IEEE conference figures.

content.text: As presented in Table IV, PRI surpasses prior approaches in both accuracy and latency. The bolded row indicates our best results. These improvements are attributable to synchronized EtherCAT exchange and the division of responsibilities between PLC sequencing and robot-native trajectory execution. The ablation study demonstrates that deterministic networking is crucial: replacing EtherCAT with standard TCP increased $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ variability and reduced task success.

We conducted a 72-hour endurance test to evaluate long-term stability. The system executed continuous cyclic pick-and-place batches with nominal conveyor loads. Key metrics tracked included failure rate, mean cycle time, and thermal trends. The endurance test recorded 99.2% reliability with 5 recoverable faults over 72 hours, yielding a measured MTBF of approximately 14.4 hours between recoverable faults. Inspection of logs showed that three faults were due to transient EtherCAT frame drops followed by automatic re-synchronization, and two were caused by minor gripper misalignments remedied by automated recalibration.

content.text: The endurance charts show stable mean cycle time and a transient temperature rise at hour 36 synchronized with an EtherCAT frame-loss event. Corrective measures included improved cable shielding and switch firmware updates. The endurance test validates the system's resilience under continuous operation and demonstrates the effectiveness of the PLC-led diagnostics and automatic resynchronization routines.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose PRI, a novel PLC-centric integration framework for articulated industrial robots that addresses determinism, safety, and maintainability. The proposed system is designed to use EtherCAT for real-time exchange and OPC-UA for supervisory telemetry, with a modular PLC program structure and clear safety demarcation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% task accuracy, mean end-to-end latency of 12.3 ms, throughput up to 480 picks/min under ideal conditions, and 99.2% reliability during a 72-hour endurance test. These metrics surpass baselines such as PLC-only and PLC+ROS bridge approaches as shown in Table IV and Fig. 8.

Despite achieving strong results, limitations remain. The current PRI demonstrator relies on vendor-specific robot motion capabilities and precomputed Jacobians; fully embedding advanced kinematic optimization within the PLC would be challenging due to computational constraints. EtherCAT frame drops—though recoverable—still occurred under specific cabling disturbances, indicating that physical layer robustness is essential. Future work will focus on three directions: (1) integrating lightweight motion optimization within PLC motion modules using fixed-point arithmetic to broaden autonomy; (2) extending the architecture to support multi-robot coordinated cells with synchronized EtherCAT topologies; and (3) developing standardized templates and certification packages to reduce integration time across industry partners. Overall, PRI provides a practical, validated path for industry practitioners aiming to adopt PLC-first robotic automation in production environments.
